nodes.title: Retail Deposits
nodes.summary: The text covers retail deposits growth, including a 13% Y-o-Y rise in savings accounts and a 17% increase in average ticket size, with premium customer share up 140 bps and NTB salary uploads up 18%. Operational improvements cut account opening time from 7 to 3 days, and the Siddhi App enhanced ease of business. Term deposit inflows rose 41% in March 2025 due to effort-based credit architecture. The bank emphasizes premiumization, targeting high-value customers and reducing lower-variant offerings. CASA share remained at 41%. The Corporate Salary Suvidha proposition expanded via Employee Reimbursement Accounts and worksite transformations, with brand partnerships and a Special Suvidha Masterclass series. Fraud prevention and regulatory features were strengthened with NSDL/UIDAI checks and geo-tagging redesign. Digital banking initiatives include lean digital savings onboarding, UIDAI facial recognition KYC, and a savings application tracker. Retail term deposits grew 14% Y-o-Y, with new digital journeys like FD booking via WhatsApp. New products include the ARISE savings account for women and the Doctors Banking Program. Branch banking expanded to 6,265 outlets, including 5,865 branches, 3 Digital Banking Units, and 13,941 ATMs, covering 692 districts. The bank promotes fair treatment, accessibility for persons with disabilities, and doorstep banking for seniors.

Transformation projects aim to digitize onboarding and improve productivity. The Siddhi mobile platform supports frontline teams. Mortgages saw sustained growth with digital home loan and e-disbursement journeys. Unsecured loan growth moderated industry-wide, but personal loans grew carefully, with most from internal customers. Education loans are being digitized. The Wheels business focuses on OEM relationships and pre-owned vehicles, with Maximus platform processing most new car loans digitally and a new two-wheeler digital journey. nodes.title: Bharat Banking
nodes.summary: Bharat Banking leverages India's economic growth, digital adoption, and financial inclusion to expand in rural and semi-urban (RuSu) markets under "Har Raah Dil Se Open." It integrates infrastructure with digital tech, growing branches to 2,736 and CSC network to 28k+, adding 250+ branches and 25+ partners. Advances and deposits grew 7% and 9% Y-o-Y in fiscal 2025. Digital transformation includes e-KYC, e-NACH, e-Sign, e-Stamp, SFDC (LOS) for Farm Mechanization, end-to-end digital MFI-retail, and Micro-loan. Future plans include onboarding three verticals in SFDC, digital Gold loan controls, and instant CASA. Initiatives include "Mandi Mitra" covering 423 Mandis, "Connecting the Dots" referral program with 97,000+ conversions, and partnerships (CSC, ITC) delivering ₹30,000 crores disbursements and 9 lakh+ liability accounts over three years. Risk and compliance focus on PSL adherence and digital collections, while financial inclusion is driven through government schemes, literacy trainings, and BC partners.

It details the Bank's credit card strategy, including customer acquisition via fee-based cards, portfolio programs, risk management, and milestones like 15 million cards and ₹226,645 crore yearly spends. Co-brand partnerships across sectors, especially the Flipkart Axis card with 4 million cards, are noted. The Bank offers cards on all four networks and launched the Primus UHNI card. Technology enhancements include digital issuance, Video KYC, and PA DSS compliance. Merchant Acquiring Business holds ~20% terminal market share, with launches like Neo for Merchants and NFC Soundbox, plus 'One Axis' cross-selling. UPI payments show 33.3% Payer PSP market share (up from 26%), 19% P2M acquiring share, 183 crore VPAs, fintech partnerships, and new lending partnerships.

nodes.title: Retail Forex and Remittance business
nodes.summary: The text covers the Bank's Retail Forex and Remittance business, detailing Forex Cards digital enhancements, corporate bulk upload, and curated offers, with a focus on student, business, and leisure segments. Inward remittance initiatives include customer segmentation, same-day credit, increased STP purpose codes and limits, enhanced Remit Money limits, Citi customer migration, and vostro partnerships. Outward remittances feature GIFT city digital remittances, API integrations, and fintech partnerships driving digital transaction growth. Regulatory compliance includes PAN validation, RBI LRS integration projects, and TCS limit revisions. The Bank handled $5.4 billion in Retail Forex volumes with ~4 lakh active customers in fiscal 2025.

nodes.title: Third Party Distribution
nodes.summary: Axis Bank is a leading distributor of third-party products including mutual funds, life, general and health insurance, National Pension System, and digital gold. It offers comprehensive investment, protection, and retirement solutions. In fiscal 2025, this business significantly contributed to retail fee income growth through partnerships, product launches, distribution strength, and digital initiatives. Mutual fund AUM stood at ₹91,661 crores with ~12 lakh customers, making it the third-largest banking distributor. The bank curates schemes via in-house research, distributes from 25 AMCs, and offers alternate investments. It provides trading via Axis Direct, sourced ~6.36 million customers (7.7 lakh added in FY25), and is a leading bancassurance player with 39% life and 11% non-life fee growth. Digital-first approach led to 13% premium growth. It secured 1.6 lakh+ NPS retail accounts, raising market share to 21% and becoming number 1 in POP space. Axis Marketplace facilitates insurance distribution, and the bank focuses on digital journeys for investment products.

nodes.title: Wealth Management
nodes.summary: The Bank's wealth management business serves diverse affluent cohorts with a focus on growing and preserving wealth through partnerships offering PMS, AIFs, debt, fixed income, and mutual funds. In FY2025, new partnerships with 3 mutual fund AMCs and 17 PMS/AIFs expanded options. Assets under management exceeded ₹1 trillion as of March 31, 2025. New SIPs grew from ~5 lakh to over 6 lakh, with ~80% via digital channels. Wealth experts, in-house economic research, and partners create goal-based investment options. Digital platforms enhanced intuitive journeys for investing in digital gold, NPS, mutual funds, insurance, and sovereign bonds via the 'open' app, contributing over ₹8,600 crores in MF gross sales (102% growth). Co-origination of MF investments via SIP with savings account opening was launched. A digital journey for simultaneous demat/trading and savings account opening opened over 1 lakh accounts in Q4 FY25. The core backend system was upgraded for larger scale.

nodes.title: Affluent Banking
nodes.summary: The text covers the Bank's 'Burgundy' affluent banking offering for HNI customers, including banking, investment, and insurance products, delivered by 550+ Relationship Managers, 475+ Premium Service Managers, and 100+ Wealth Specialists across 350+ branches in India, extending to tier 2 and 3 cities. It highlights the NRI segment as key to premiumisation, serviced by 450+ dedicated NRI RMs and 300+ virtual RMs, with products and digital investment options for wealth creation in India. It introduces 'The Burgundy Promise' with three pillars—defining commitment, measuring performance, and transparent communication—offering quick resolution within a 6-working-hour TAT and real-time tracking. Finally, it mentions the Bank's new license as a distributor of capital market products at its IFSC Banking Unit (Gift City) to serve NRI investors in India and Resident Indians seeking geographic and currency diversification.

nodes.title: Private Banking
nodes.summary: The text covers Burgundy Private's growth, including expansion to tier-2 cities, customer assets, One Axis synergies, events, investment education, partner strength, and awards. It also details Priority Sector Lending (PSL) strategy, agriculture and MSME focus, Bharat Bank, partnerships, PSLC transactions, and achievement of PSL targets. Finally, it introduces Digital Banking as a strategic initiative with investments in digital capabilities.

nodes.title: Priority Sector Lending
nodes.summary: The text covers Burgundy Private's brand identity and its partnership with Hurun India for the 4th edition of the 'Burgundy Private Hurun India 500 Most Valuable Companies' in February 2025. It then details Priority Sector Lending (PSL), explaining its regulatory mandate to direct credit to underserved sectors like agriculture, MSMEs, affordable housing, education, and renewable energy for inclusive growth. The Bank achieved its overall PSL targets in fiscal 2025, with a focus on becoming self-sufficient in agriculture credit through the Bharat Bank strategy, which includes products like crop loans, KCC, and farm infrastructure loans. The Bank expanded rural and semi-urban presence, supported rural MSMEs, and used partnerships with NBFCs/MFIs via co-lending and securitisation. It augmented small-ticket loans, crop loans, and microfinance for women, and enhanced digital lending for MSMEs. PSL achievement was ~48.5% against a 40% target, with PSLC purchases and sales. Finally, the text highlights Digital Banking as a key initiative, with the Bank's fully digital bank under Axis 2.0 and investments in proprietary digital capabilities for consumer lending.

nodes.title: Digital Banking
nodes.summary: The text covers the Bank's management discussion, including the Burgundy Private brand and its Hurun India partnership. It details Priority Sector Lending (PSL): definition, fiscal 2025 achievement of ~48.5% against a 40% target, use of PSLC purchases and sales, and strategies like the Bharat Bank initiative, agricultural products (KCC), MSME lending, partnerships with NBFCs/MFIs, co-lending, securitisation, and digital lending enhancements. It then discusses Digital Banking: Axis 2.0 rebranded as 'Open by Axis Bank', in-house engineering, mobile app ratings (4.7/4.8) and 15 million monthly active users, over 30 digital products, new offerings (My Money, FD via UPI, One-view), 6% business contribution with 47% deposit and 15% loan growth, digital lending progress, personalization, Project Neo for wholesale banking, Neo for Business (1.8 lakh registrations), 135 Open Banking APIs, Neo for Corporates, and Axis Neo Connect.

nodes.title: Wholesale Banking and products
nodes.summary: The Bank's Wholesale Banking franchise addresses all corporate banking needs through innovative strategies for growth. In fiscal 2025, it focused on deeper client relationships and comprehensive solutions using the 'One Axis' approach across segments and subsidiaries. The Wholesale Coverage Group offers products including cash credit, loans, project finance, export credit, trade services, forex, derivatives, cash management, tax payments, salary accounts, trust services, and cards, supported by a dedicated products team for customized solutions. It serves SMEs, start-ups, large and mid-corporates, MNCs, financial institutions, PSUs, and government departments via a sharpened structure: Mid-Corporates & Medium Enterprises Group (turnover ₹100–1,500 crores), Large Corporates (turnover >₹1,500 crores), and Focused Segmental Coverage for PSUs, government entities, MNCs, start-ups, real economy corporates, and financial institutions.

nodes.title: Wholesale Banking Coverage Group
nodes.summary: The Wholesale Banking Coverage Group solidified its position as a preferred transaction bank across current accounts, cash management, trade finance, capital markets, and custody, serving 70% of unicorns and 40% of Series A+ start-ups with tailored solutions like escrow, APIs, and the Axis Start-Up Card. It leads in domestic payment gateways and is expanding cross-border via PACB. The Real Economy Group doubled business in two years, contributing 50% to syndication volumes, and leads in local currency loans. It supports clean energy and InvITs/REITs. MEG expands NEO for Business with AI. Key deals include India's first Blue loan ($500M from IFC) and a UTI MF custody deal doubling AUC to ₹10 lakh crore. WBCG organized a Defence Conclave and integrated with the Upyog platform. IT & GCC COE serves 1,000+ MNCs with 32% CAGR. The Bank is poised to capture growth from ₹11 lakh crore government capex, ₹3.5 trillion private capex, and PLI schemes, focusing on efficiency and sustainable growth.

nodes.title: Commercial Banking Coverage Group (CBG)
nodes.summary: The text covers the Commercial Banking Coverage Group (CBG) and its role in serving MSMEs with tailored banking solutions across loans, trade/forex, liabilities, and fee products. It highlights CBG's geographical presence with 155 MSME centres, a book of ₹1.19 lakh crores, and its contribution as a PSL engine. It discusses innovation through digital platforms like 'NEO for Business' and strategic partnerships. The text also details Wholesale Banking Products, including 'NEO by Axis Bank' digital offerings, cash management solutions (payment hub, NEFT/IMPS leadership, tax collection, Bharat Connect), and commercial cards with innovations for sole proprietors and B2B payments.

nodes.title: Wholesale Banking, Cash Management and CBG Overview
nodes.summary: The page covers CBG's wide geographical presence with 155 MSME centres, a book of ₹1.19 lakh crores, and its role as a PSL engine. It highlights innovation through digital platforms like 'NEO for Business' with AI analytics, and strategic partnerships for geographic penetration. Wholesale Banking Products section details the Bank's transaction banking leadership across current accounts, cash management, trade finance, capital markets, and custody, featuring 'NEO by Axis Bank' with APIs, corporate internet banking, and host-to-host integration. Cash Management covers comprehensive solutions, a new payment hub doubling NEFT speed, leadership in NEFT/IMPS processing, customized MT940 and API-based statements for reconciliation, authorization for Direct Taxes, GST and Custom Duty collection with card/UPI gateway, and leadership in Bharat Connect (BBPS) with new categories like Prepaid Electricity Meter and NPS.

nodes.title: Commercial Cards
nodes.summary: The text covers Commercial Cards, including tailored payment solutions, digitization, a card for sole proprietors, 24/7 phone banking, digital onboarding, and leadership in B2B and statutory payments. Trade and Supply Chain Finance offers domestic and international products via branches and digital channels with system integration, supported by product specialists for exports, imports, bank guarantees, working capital, liquidity, and risk management. It details international trade solutioning (LC confirmation for high-risk geographies, partnerships for auto/oil exporters, Gift City products, ERP-EDPMS reconciliation) and structured trade initiatives (back-to-back LCs, energy sector deal from Dubai). Current Account focuses on transaction banking growth, service excellence, BOTF, Re-KYC journeys, and customized propositions for sectors like FMCG, real estate, pharma, tourism, IT, e-commerce, education, FPOs, and digital merchant accounts. Treasury & Markets comprises ALM (CRR, SLR, LCR, NSFR, liquidity/interest/currency risk under ALCO), Forex Trading (proprietary trading, market making), Interest Rate Trading (G-Sec, OIS, primary dealership, bidding commitments), Non-SLR Trading (corporate bonds, CPs, CDs, equity), DCM, Treasury Sales, Loan Syndication, and Treasury Technology & Governance.

nodes.title: Trade and Supply Chain Finance and Current Account Overview
nodes.summary: The page covers Trade and Supply Chain Finance, detailing comprehensive domestic and international products via branch and digital channels, with dedicated product specialists. It highlights international trade solutions like confirming LCs for exporters to lower-rated geographies, partnerships for Auto and Oil exporters, new Gift City branch products, and ERP-EDPMS reconciliation. Structured Trade initiatives include a specialized team, back-to-back LCs, and an energy sector deal from Dubai. The Bank is expanding integrated supply chain solutions. Current Account focuses on growth, service excellence, self-service channel penetration, BOTF, Re-KYC journeys, and customized propositions for sectors like FMCG, Real estate, Pharma, Tourism, IT, E-commerce, Education, and FPOs, plus digital merchant offerings.

nodes.title: Treasury & Markets
nodes.summary: The Treasury & Markets function comprises ALM, Forex Trading, Interest Rate Trading, Non-SLR Trading, Debt Capital Markets, Treasury Sales, Loan Syndication, and Treasury Technology & Governance. ALM manages CRR, SLR, LCR, NFSR, and liquidity, interest rate, and currency risks under ALCO. Forex Trading undertakes proprietary trading and market making in forex and derivatives. IRT handles market making in G-Sec, OIS, and other interest rate products; as a primary dealer, it ensures bidding commitments, success ratio, and turnover ratio for T-bill and G-Sec auctions. Non-SLR Trading covers corporate bonds, commercial papers, certificates of deposits, and equity. DCM is a dominant player with domestic and international franchises, ranking first in CY2024 and maintaining leadership for 16 years until 2022, including ESG-compliant issuances. Treasury Sales provides bespoke risk management and hedging solutions and offers the 'Neo for Markets' digital proposition. Loan Syndication arranges loan facilities and conducts secondary loan sales/purchases. TTG oversees treasury technology implementation and governance. The Bank transitioned to Murex as its core treasury system for all products except Bullion.

nodes.title: Customer Obsession (SPARSH)
nodes.summary:
Customer Obsession (SPARSH)
Sparsh, our Customer Obsession program, is a Bank-wide priority and a core area of distinctiveness for us, the tenets of which are now ingrained across all our 5,800+ branches, every customer touchpoint, and amongst all our 1.04 lakh+ colleagues. The journey toward customer obsession commenced at Axis Bank with an extensive outside-in effort, encompassing surveys of over 12,000 customers, conducting over 1,000 employee discussions, and evaluating more than 50 global companies for benchmarking purposes.

nodes.title: Sparsh 2.0: Enhancing Customer Satisfaction and Business Outcomes
nodes.summary: Sparsh 2.0 aims to enhance customer satisfaction, NPS, and business outcomes through key focus areas: regional restructuring with Sparsh Labs for feedback; fostering a listening culture; improving input metrics like TAT and FTR; agile customer service via real-time NPS close looping; low-cost WOW moments; identifying input metrics for business results; increasing products per customer for loyalty; and driving customer advocacy. The Bank's four building blocks for customer obsession are crafting delight journeys, embedding Sparsh values in all employees, measuring and acting on customer feedback, and building institutional capabilities like Axis Promise and tech tools Adi and Kaleidoscope.

nodes.title: Business Intelligence Unit
nodes.summary: The Business Intelligence Unit (BIU) is a high-impact team using data to drive decisions across marketing, risk, strategy, collections, and fraud for retail, wholesale, and commercial banking. With over 740 experts in data engineering, data science, Gen AI, and strategic analysis, the bank has invested in a new operating model with skill mapping and new-age roles. Focus on Gen AI, ML, and analytics enables data-driven decisions, supported by investments in big data, cloud, microservices, and analytics platforms. The modern data stack includes 2,000+ live use cases on a petabyte-scale lakehouse, with MDM for data quality and DPDPA compliance. Key initiatives include optimization analytics (10,000+ simulations), ML engineering (25% faster model development), and Gen AI for automation and productivity.

nodes.title: Information Technology and Cyber Security
nodes.summary: The text outlines the Bank's IT and cyber security strategy, emphasizing a vision aligned with becoming a leading tech and digital bank. It covers IT capabilities with a 2,000+ member team, 35+ key initiatives like lending transformation, GenAI, personalization, digital payments, and cloud integration. Mobile Banking features 250+ functionalities, 4.8/4.7 ratings, 33.7 million registered users, and 15 million monthly active users. It highlights support in 10+ languages, 32 digital services on BOTF, and WhatsApp banking with 30 million customers. UPI leadership includes a 1,674 million VPA base, 33% market share, and new UPI ATM features. GenAI initiatives include Axis Deep Intelligence, 4,500+ bots, and 1,850+ automated processes. API platform details 840+ partner APIs, 2,000+ internal APIs, and 50% increased daily requests. Cloud-first approach with 150+ applications, ISO certifications, and zero trust controls. Infrastructure spans two data centers with DR, compliance, and security measures. CBDC initiatives include 0.65 million customers and 6 million transactions. Cyber security framework aligns with NIST and ISO27001, ISO27017, ISO27034, ISO27018, and PCIDSS, featuring 24/7 SOC, BitSight rating of 810, zero-trust architecture, and various controls. Governance framework includes Board, Risk Management Committee, IT & Digital Strategy Committee, and Information System Security Committee. Risk management objectives focus on risk-sensitive operations, robust governance, independent function, board-approved appetite, and risk culture.

nodes.title: Risk
nodes.summary: The text outlines the Bank's cybersecurity framework aligned with NIST and ISO standards, detailing compliance certifications, 24/7 Security Operations Centre, Dark Net monitoring, BitSight rating, and internal controls like zero-trust architecture, micro-segmentation, DLP, DevSecOps, and SaaS/PaaS vetting. It describes the Enterprise Security Governance Framework with strategic oversight by the Board and Risk Management Committee, and executive oversight by IT & Digital Strategy Committee and Information System Security Committee. The risk management section covers objectives, enablers (governance, independence, appetite, culture), Board and committee oversight, independent risk function led by a Chief Risk Officer, risk appetite framework, and initiatives to strengthen risk culture.

nodes.title: Risk Governance, Independent Risk Function, and Risk Appetite Overview
nodes.summary: The page covers risk governance, the independent risk management function, and risk appetite. It details the Board's oversight and its committees, including the Risk Management Committee, Audit Committee, and others, plus executive risk committees and their oversight. It explains the independent risk function's assurance role, the Chief Risk Officer's independence enablers such as board appointment, no business targets, direct committee access, and involvement in decision-making bodies. Finally, it describes the risk appetite's approval by the Risk Management Committee, its framework guiding management, cascading to business units, and monitoring by the Risk Department with reporting to senior management and the committee.

nodes.title: Risk Culture
nodes.summary:
Risk Culture
A robust operational risk and compliance culture is the cornerstone for risk management in any institution. In the Bank, Risk Department along with Compliance Department has put in place an action plan to strengthen the risk and compliance culture. This includes various initiatives such as -
263Statutory reports
• Training and awareness programs • Strengthening staff accountability framework • Clarity on roles and responsibilities of the front line staff • Tone from the top through communication from the MD & CEO

nodes.title: Risk Architecture
nodes.summary:
Risk Architecture
The risk architecture is composed, for every type of risk, of elements of - • Governance with executive risk committee oversight • Risk policies to provide guidance • Tools for measuring risk level • Monitoring of risk profile • Reporting for actioning A summary of these facets of the key risks is provided here:
Risk type
Definition

nodes.title: Approach to risk management
nodes.summary: The text outlines the Bank's approach to risk management, covering credit risk (definition, sources, and management via internal ratings, scorecards, and validation), market risk (definition, sources from trading/investment activities, and management using statistical measures like VaR, stress tests, and non-statistical measures like position limits), combined management of traded credit products, and a comprehensive market risk framework for banking and trading books. It also defines liquidity risk and details its management through ALM policy, gap analysis, stress testing, and Basel III liquidity standards (LCR/NSFR). Finally, it covers operational risk, including its sources and manifestations (core process, change management, outsourcing, continuity, and information/cyber security risks) and the ORM policy, risk measurement system, and committees for change management and outsourcing.

nodes.title: Risk Types, Liquidity Risk, Operational Risk, and Risk Management Approach
nodes.summary: The page defines liquidity risk as a bank's inability to meet obligations and operational risk as arising from inadequate controls in processes, people, systems, or external events, manifesting in core process, change management, outsourcing, continuity, and information/cyber security risks. It details the bank's risk management approach: historical simulation VaR at 99% confidence, backtesting, stress tests, and ALM policy for liquidity risk with governance, monitoring, and Basel III integration (LCR/NSFR). Core operational risk is managed via an ORM Policy and measurement system. Change management risk involves risk evaluation of new/changed products by the Operational Risk team, with oversight by Product and Change Management Committees. Outsourcing risk is approved by the Outsourcing Committee after Operational Risk team recommendations.

nodes.title: Outsourcing risk
nodes.summary: This text defines liquidity risk as a bank's inability to meet cash and collateral obligations without unacceptable losses, and operational risk as arising from inadequate internal processes, people, systems, or external events, manifesting in core process, change management, outsourcing, continuity, and information/cyber security risks. It details the bank's risk management approach: historical simulation VaR (99% confidence, one-day holding, 250-day horizon) with backtesting, stress tests, and sensitivity analyses; an ALM Policy for liquidity risk governance, stress testing, and contingency funding, supplemented by intraday and overseas branch policies; periodic gap analysis and liquidity ratio monitoring reviewed by ALCO and the Risk Management Committee; and integration of RBI Basel III liquidity standards (LCR/NSFR). It also covers the ORM Policy for operational risk assessment and monitoring, the Operational Risk Measurement System, risk evaluation of new products/processes by the Operational Risk team and committees, and Outsourcing Committee approval of outsourcing arrangements.

nodes.title: Approach to risk management Business continuity risk
nodes.summary:
Approach to risk management Business continuity risk
The Business Continuity Planning Management Committee (BCPMC) exercises oversight on the implementation of the approved Business Continuity Plan (BCP) framework which has been put in place to ensure continuity of service to its large customer base. The effectiveness of the approved Business Continuity Plan (BCP) framework is tested for all identified critical internal activities to ensure readiness to meet various contingency scenarios. The learning from the BCP exercises are used as inputs to further refine the framework. With effective Business Continuity Plan in place, the Bank has effectively managed to run its operations by adapting to various continuity/mitigation plans.

nodes.title: Information security risk
nodes.summary: The text covers the Bank's information security risk management, detailing a holistic program with policies aligned to NIST, ISO27001, and PCI DSS. It describes governance via an Information System Security Committee, technical and administrative controls, compliance with ISO27001 and PCI DSS, various security assessments, defense in depth, a 24x7 SOC, and coordination with RBI, CERT-IN, NCIIPC, and NPCI. It then discusses management's discussion and analysis for fiscal 2025, highlighting strategic initiatives to strengthen risk infrastructure, including group risk governance, model risk, operational risk controls, technology resilience, digital banking, and risk culture. It also mentions the Risk Department's four areas of distinctiveness: climate/ESG risk, cyber security training, retail lending models, and rural lending toolkits. Finally, it briefly notes subsidiary governance within Axis Group as a Financial Conglomerate, with a framework approved by the Risk Management Committee and Board, and the role of the Subsidiary Governance Department.

nodes.title: a. alignment of important policies by the subsidiaries with group wide policies & best practices; and
nodes.summary: The text covers subsidiary governance, compliance, internal audit, CSR & sustainability, ESG, and human resources. It details policy alignment, reporting frameworks, and oversight by executive and board committees. Compliance focuses on regulatory adherence, risk management, and technology use. Internal audit operates independently, using risk-based audits and emerging technologies. CSR initiatives span education, healthcare, sports, environment, and livelihoods, with achievements like planting 3.27 million saplings and impacting 2.05 million participants. ESG covers sustainable financing, climate risk, and diversity commitments. HR highlights training, culture, talent mobility, campus hiring, performance recognition, DEI, well-being, and flexible work models.

nodes.title: Conclusion
nodes.summary: The text concludes Axis Bank's commitment to an inclusive, high-performance, employee-centric workplace through strategic HR initiatives. It details subsidiary performance under the 'One Axis' strategy focused on growth, profitability, and sustainability, highlighting Axis Capital's ECM leadership, Axis AMC's growth and ranking, Axis Finance's AUF CAGR and returns, and overall subsidiary net profit and ROI. Individual subsidiaries are profiled: Axis Capital's deal count and earnings growth; Axis AMC's folios, AUM, and pension fund AUM; Axis Securities' client base, earnings, and trading volume growth; Axis Finance's diversification, capital adequacy, and asset quality; Freecharge's digital solutions, expansion, and UPI GMV growth; and A.TReDs' invoice financing and participant metrics. It includes a safe harbor statement on forward-looking statements and an independent auditor's certificate on corporate governance compliance.

nodes.title: OPINION
nodes.summary: The text is an auditor's certificate confirming the Bank's compliance with Corporate Governance Regulations for the year ended 31 March 2025, based on examined records and management representations. It clarifies that compliance does not assure future viability or management efficiency. The certificate is restricted for use solely by the Bank's Members to meet regulatory requirements, with no liability accepted for other purposes or persons, and no responsibility to update for subsequent events. It concludes with the auditor's signature, firm details, and date.

nodes.title: Report on Corporate Governance
nodes.summary: The Report on Corporate Governance covers Axis Bank's governance philosophy, structure, and Board details, including composition, independence, diversity, and effectiveness. It details Board and Committee meetings, performance evaluation, and remuneration policies for directors and employees. It discloses fees paid to statutory auditors, confirms no preferential allotment funds raised, and reports sexual harassment disclosures and zero employee accidental deaths. It outlines the Whistleblower Policy, subsidiary oversight, material subsidiary policy, D&O insurance, and insider trading compliance. It includes compliance and CEO/CFO certifications, Directors E-KYC, related party transactions, senior management changes, non-compliance instances, codes of conduct, ESG initiatives, and vendor onboarding processes.

nodes.title: I. Philosophy on Code of Governance
nodes.summary: Axis Bank Limited recognizes its role as a responsible corporate citizen and commits to the highest standards of corporate governance. Its philosophy promotes customer centricity, ownership, integrity, sustainability, transparency, and ethics in stakeholder dealings. The Bank maintains a robust governance structure led by an independent and diverse Board of Directors, emphasizing prompt and clear stakeholder communication reflected in internal functioning. It aims to exceed legal requirements with best-in-class practices, supported by a strong compliance and risk management framework, and continuously reviews practices and processes in light of the dynamic environment to protect stakeholder interests.

nodes.title: II. Governance Structure of the Bank
nodes.summary: The text outlines the Bank's governance structure, detailing the Board's oversight of corporate governance and director appointment by members. It describes reporting lines: the Managing Director & CEO reports to the Board, while the Deputy Managing Director and Executive Directors report to the MD & CEO. It lists various Board-level Committees for focused review and executive Committees for routine, operational, and administrative matters. A diagrammatic representation includes the Board of Directors, MD & CEO, Executive Directors, Independent Directors, Nominee Director, Deputy MD, Board Committees, Group Executives, and specific committees such as the Audit Committee, Risk Management Committee, Committee of Directors, ESG Committee, Customer Service Committee, Nomination and Remuneration Committee, Stakeholders Relationship Committee, Special Committee for Fraud Monitoring, Review Committee, CSR Committee, Committee of Whole-Time Directors, IT and Digital Strategy Committee, and Acquisitions, Divestments and Mergers Committee.

nodes.title: III. Board of Directors
nodes.summary: The section details the Board of Directors, including its size and composition (thirteen directors as of March 31, 2025, with an independent part-time chairman, executives, independent directors, and a nominee director, meeting statutory and regulatory requirements), independence criteria, average tenure, and gender diversity. It covers Board effectiveness in strategic planning, risk management, HR, audit, governance, and financial inclusion. It also addresses the databank of independent directors, fit and proper compliance, director selection and appointment processes, succession planning policy, board diversity policy, training and induction programmes, familiarisation and CELP programmes, duties and responsibilities of the Board, roles of independent directors, and specific roles of the Chairman, MD & CEO, Deputy MD, and Executive Directors. It notes policy amendments during fiscal 2025 and compliance with applicable laws and regulations.

nodes.title: Board of Directors: Size, Composition, and Effectiveness
key_items: Size and composition of the Board
nodes.summary: The page covers the Board of Directors, detailing its size and composition in compliance with the Companies Act, SEBI Listing Regulations, Banking Regulation Act, RBI guidelines, and the Bank's Articles of Association. It describes the Board's composition as of March 31, 2025, with thirteen directors including executives, independent directors, and a nominee director, led by an independent part-time chairman. It notes that independent directors exceed half the total strength, and all meet independence criteria. The page also includes data on average tenure and gender diversity, and discusses Board effectiveness in areas such as strategic planning, risk management, human resources, audit, governance, and financial inclusion.

nodes.title: Databank of Independent Directors
nodes.summary: The text covers multiple aspects of corporate governance at a bank: compliance of Independent Directors with the Companies (Appointment and Qualification of Directors) Rules, 2014 regarding enrollment in the online databank and proficiency self-assessment test; detailed information about directors, including name, category, DIN, age, date of first appointment, end date of current term, directorships in other listed/unlisted companies, memberships/chairpersonships of Board committees, and shareholding; certification that all directors are compliant and fit and proper; and descriptions of policies for selection and appointment of directors, including the Succession Planning Policy for the Board and key officials, the Policy on Fit and Proper Criteria for Directors, and related processes such as succession planning, board diversity, training, and external consultant engagement. The text also notes amendments to the succession planning policy during fiscal 2025 and the NRC's annual fit and proper assessment.

nodes.title: Director Selection, Fitness Compliance, and Succession Planning Policy
key_items: Process of Selection and Appointment of Directors
Succession Planning Policy for the Board and Key Officials of the Bank
nodes.summary: The page covers statutory reports confirming all directors submitted required declarations and are fit and proper per NRC and Board review. It details the process for selecting and appointing directors, referencing policies on fit and proper criteria, board diversity, and training, including reviewing succession needs, identifying candidates, assessing suitability, and conducting induction and education. It then describes the Succession Planning Policy for the Board and key officials, outlining its objective to identify and nominate candidates for various leadership roles, plan for vacancies, develop competencies through training, and handle delays or sudden vacancies. It notes the policy excludes Non-Executive Nominee Directors, explains NRC's role in evaluating profiles and engaging external consultants, and mentions Board-approved amendments during fiscal 2025.

nodes.title: Policy on fit and proper criteria for Directors of the Bank
nodes.summary: The text outlines the Bank's policy on fit and proper criteria for Directors. It details that the NRC assesses and confirms Directors' fit and proper status before appointment/re-appointment and annually as of March 31. The policy's primary objective is to ensure candidates comply with fit and proper norms before NRC recommendation to the Board. Directors must sign a deed of covenant to be eligible for appointment/re-appointment. The Bank obtains annual declarations and undertakings on fit and proper criteria per RBI Regulations and IRDAI (Registration of Corporate Agent) Regulations, 2015, from all Directors. During fiscal 2025, the Board reviewed and approved amendments to the policy in line with extant laws.

nodes.title: Board Diversity Policy
nodes.summary: The text outlines the Bank's Board Diversity Policy, emphasizing the importance of a diverse Board with a balance of skills and perspectives for effective governance. It lists mandated core skills for the Board and details each Director's experience and competencies. The policy is reviewed annually and available on the website. Additionally, it covers the Bank's training policy for Directors, including induction programs for new Directors, familiarization programs, and Continuous Education and Learning Programs (CELP), which are conducted to keep Directors informed about business, regulatory, and operational aspects. The policy is in line with SEBI Listing Regulations and was reviewed in fiscal 2025.

nodes.title: Directors' Experience, Board Training, and Induction Programme
key_items: Familiarisation and Training for the Board
nodes.summary: The page lists directors' total experience and expertise areas, with a combined total experience of 507 years, and references the bank's website for detailed profiles. It outlines the Board's training policy covering induction for new directors and familiarisation/CELP programmes, reviewed in fiscal 2025. The induction programme includes one-to-one meetings with senior management on businesses, credit, finance, strategy, risk, compliance, audit, HR, IT/cyber security, ESG, CSR, law, treasury, subsidiary governance, and board processes, plus an induction manual with governance policies. Independent Directors receive appointment letters detailing terms, conditions, duties, and responsibilities, with the format available on the bank's website.

nodes.title: Familiarisation programme and Continuous Education and Learning Programme (CELP) for Directors

These programmes, led by internal experts and external agencies, are tailored to business needs, existing skills, and Director recommendations, providing insights into contemporary matters. In fiscal 2025, 13 programmes were held for around 14 hours, covering topics such as emerging technologies, AI/ML in banking, cybersecurity, geopolitics, board governance, digital banking, economic outlook, AML, risk management, Indian banking, credit cycles, and Gen AI. Details and attendance are uploaded on the Bank's website.

nodes.title: Duties and Responsibilities of the Board

It describes the Board's review processes, including quarterly performance reviews and annual long-term strategy meetings, and its oversight of management to enhance shareholder value. It notes the Board's discretion to hire external advisors and mentions the charter outlining duties, which was amended in fiscal 2025.

nodes.title: Role of Independent Directors

It identifies the key managerial personnel. It also covers the framework for Board and Committee meetings, including scheduling, conduct standards, agenda preparation, and the use of a secured portal for document distribution, with emphasis on RBI's seven critical themes and compliance with legal provisions.

nodes.title: Roles of Chairman, MD & CEO, Deputy MD, and Executive Directors
nodes.summary: The page outlines the roles of key leadership positions at the Bank. The Independent Chairman facilitates effective Board functioning and presides over shareholder, Board, and committee meetings. The Managing Director & CEO manages the Bank's affairs under Board supervision with delegated authority. The Deputy Managing Director oversees wholesale banking, treasury, digital banking, marketing, and communications. Two Executive Directors report to the MD & CEO: one handles banking operations, transformation, IT, and strategy; the other drives business growth across products and financial inclusion. All four are identified as key managerial personnel under Section 203(1) of the Act.

nodes.title: IV. Meetings of the Board / Committees
nodes.summary: This section covers the Board and Committee meetings of the Bank, including the schedule and framework for conducting meetings, agenda preparation, information flow to the Board, follow-up and monitoring mechanisms, the annual Board Strategy Meet, and minutes. It details compliance with Rule 3, the nine Board meetings and the 30th AGM attendance. It notes no Independent Director resigned. It lists 13 Board Committees, their composition, charters, quorum, and meeting attendance, covering COD, ACB, RMC, SRC, NRC, SCBMF, CSC, ITDSC, CSR Committee, Review Committee, ADAM, COWTD, and ESG Committee, along with the Management Committee and separate Independent Directors' meetings, including the Board Performance Evaluation process.

nodes.summary:
IV. Meetings of the Board / Committees
Schedule of the meetings
The schedule of the meetings of the Board / Committees and the Annual General Meeting of the Bank to be held during the next fiscal, is finalised and circulated in advance to the Board.
Framework for conduct of meetings of the Board / Committees
The Bank has formulated and adopted a framework for conduct of meetings of the Board / Committees of the Bank.
The said framework provides guidance on matters relating to administration of meetings by ensuring standardization in the formats used for preparation of agenda index, agenda notes, minutes and circular resolutions and adopting best practices from a compliance and governance perspective.

nodes.title: Agenda for the meetings
nodes.summary: The RBI circular prescribes seven critical themes for Board review, and meeting agendas cover these plus statutory matters, finalized with chairpersons and circulated via a secure portal. Information to the Board includes structured agenda notes on business, risk, CSR, ESG, minutes, appointments, and compliance. A post-meeting follow-up communicates decisions for action, with a monitoring framework periodically reviewed by Executive Director Subrat Mohanty and quarterly by the Board. The annual three-day Board Strategy Meet focuses on long-term strategy, risk, and financial planning. Minutes are drafted within 15 days, signed at the next meeting, with a GCI framework, and resolutions by circulation for urgent matters. Meetings comply with Rule 3, with nine Board meetings and strategy meet dates listed.

nodes.title: Corporate Governance: Board Information, Follow-up, Monitoring, Strategy and Minutes

Framework for monitoring and implementation of the directions of the Board

nodes.summary: The page covers corporate governance disclosures, including a certificate from Secretarial Auditors confirming no directors are debarred or disqualified by SEBI, MCA, or other authorities, annexed to the Board's Report. It states compliance with SEBI Listing Regulations 17 to 27, clauses (b) to (i) of Regulation 46(2), and paragraphs C, D, and E of Schedule V, plus all mandatory requirements. It lists adopted non-mandatory requirements: Chairperson's office maintenance, separate Chairperson and MD & CEO, unmodified audit opinions, Chief Audit Executive reporting to ACB, and independent directors' meetings. A Joint Statutory Auditors' certificate confirms corporate governance compliance for fiscal 2025, annexed at the report's start. No agreements under Regulation 30A(1) were reported during fiscal 2025, so no disclosure is required.

nodes.title: Codes of Conduct
nodes.summary: The text covers the Bank's Codes of Conduct, including Board and employee codes under SEBI Listing Regulations, emphasizing integrity, ethics, and core values (customer centricity, ethics, transparency, teamwork, ownership). Employees annually affirm compliance, and prior approval is needed for outside positions. The codes are hosted on the website, with a CEO certificate attached. It describes the Governance Compliance Manager system for tracking regulatory changes and compliance assessments reported to the ACB and Board. Sustainability efforts include an ESG Committee, policies like ESG Lending and Sustainable Financing Framework, disclosures aligned with GRI, IR, and TCFD, and a $500 million IFC partnership for blue finance. Vendor processes cover a vendor onboarding policy, platform, and Supplier Code of Conduct with an online concern-reporting mechanism.

nodes.title: Compliance, Sustainability, and Statutory Reports Overview
nodes.summary: The page covers statutory reports, noting the Bank's codes are hosted online per SEBI Listing Regulations, with a CEO certificate confirming director and senior management compliance attached as Annexure 2. Compliance details the Governance Compliance Manager system for tracking and implementing regulatory changes, with the compliance department conducting independent assessments and reporting to the ACB and Board. Sustainability highlights the Bank's ESG focus, including the first Indian bank's Board-level ESG Committee established in 2021, policies like the ESG Lending Policy and Sustainable Financing Framework, disclosures aligned with GRI, IR, and TCFD, and a fiscal 2025 partnership with IFC for a $500 million blue finance and green projects loan.

nodes.title: Vendor Processes and Supplier Code of Conduct
nodes.summary: The text covers the Bank's vendor onboarding policy, including identification, selection, and an online platform for proposals, with vendors evaluated per set principles. It outlines the Supplier Code of Conduct, detailing minimum ethical standards, supplier reporting of concerns via an online mechanism, and the goal of ethical business relationships for sustainable benefits. It also includes CEO/CFO certification under SEBI Regulation 17(8) confirming financial statements' accuracy, no fraudulent transactions, internal control responsibility, and disclosures to auditors. Finally, it confirms compliance with the Code of Conduct and conflict of interest norms by directors and senior management for fiscal 2025.

nodes.title: General Shareholder Information
nodes.summary: This section provides comprehensive general shareholder information for Axis Bank, covering contact details for registered/corporate offices, debenture trustees, registrar (KFIN), and GDR depository; AGM and e-voting details, dividend declaration and payment procedures, record dates, and financial year calendar. It lists stock exchange details for equity, GDRs/ADRs, debt securities, and MTN bonds, along with listing fees, depositories, and confirmation of no outstanding convertible warrants. Dividend payment processes, including electronic modes, KYC requirements, unclaimed dividend and IEPF transfer procedures, and dematerialisation status are detailed. Shareholding pattern, credit ratings, investor services, complaint redressal, and correspondence are presented. Procedures for physical share requests, dispute resolution, nomination, green initiatives, means of communication, RTA evaluation, general meetings, postal ballot details, commodity risk hedging, and plant locations are also included.

nodes.title: Axis Bank General Shareholder Information and Contact Details
key_items: Registrar & Share Transfer Agent (“RTA”) KFin Technologies Limited (“KFIN”)
nodes.summary: The page provides general shareholder information for Axis Bank Limited, including contact details for its Registered Office, Corporate Office, Debenture Trustees (IDBI Trusteeship Services Limited and SBICAP Trustee Company Limited), Registrar & Share Transfer Agent (KFin Technologies Limited), and Depository for Global Depository Receipts (The Bank of New York Mellon). It also covers details about the 31st Annual General Meeting scheduled for Friday, 25 July 2025, at 10:00 am via Video Conferencing, e-voting dates from 4 July to 24 July 2025, dividend amount of ₹1 per share, record date of 21 July 2025, dividend payment within 30 days of the AGM, financial year from 1 April to 31 March, and a meeting calendar.

nodes.title: Purpose
nodes.summary: The text outlines the tentative schedule for the Bank's financial results announcements for quarters ending June 2025, September 2025, December 2025, and the fiscal year ending March 2026. It then lists stock exchange details for equity shares (BSE, NSE), GDRs/ADRs (London Stock Exchange), debt securities (BSE, NSE), and MTN bonds (London, Singapore, India INX, NSE IFSC), including ISINs, codes, and addresses. It notes no suspended trading, GDR/ADR issuance details, and no outstanding convertible warrants. It covers listing fees, depositories (NSDL, CDSL), and dividend payment procedures via electronic mode, including requirements for members to provide bank details and handling of rejected payments.

nodes.title: Stock Exchange Details, Convertible Warrants, Listing Fees, and Depositories
nodes.summary: The page lists stock exchange details for London, Singapore, India International, and NSE IFSC, including addresses and websites. It states that as of 31 March 2025, the Bank has no outstanding convertible warrants. It notes that annual listing fees for fiscal 2025 have been paid to the stock exchanges. Finally, it identifies NSDL and CDSL as depositories for the Bank's equity shares and confirms payment of annual custodian fees for fiscal 2025 to the depositories.

nodes.title: Payment of Dividend
nodes.summary: The text covers SEBI regulations mandating electronic dividend payments via RBI-approved modes, requiring members to provide bank details, email, and mobile numbers. It details procedures for physical shareholders and consequences of rejected electronic payments. SEBI's mandate for KYC updates for physical securities is highlighted, with dividend withholding for non-compliant folios. Unclaimed dividend provisions under the Companies Act and IEPF Rules are explained, including transfer of unclaimed dividends to IEPF, a table of unclaimed amounts for fiscals 2017-18 to 2023-24 with claim deadlines, and reminders sent. Finally, it addresses transfer of underlying equity shares to IEPF for unclaimed dividends over seven years, with shares transferred up to 31 March, 2025.

nodes.title: Unclaimed Dividend
nodes.summary: SEBI mandates that physical securities holders with incomplete KYC (PAN, nomination, contact details, bank details, specimen signature) will receive payments like dividends only electronically from April 1, 2024, and dividends may be withheld otherwise. Unclaimed dividend for seven years must be transferred to IEPF; `1,18,04,460 from fiscal 2017 was transferred on September 25, 2024. Unclaimed dividend as of March 31, 2025, for fiscals 2017-18 to 2023-24 totals `88,68,728, with fiscal-wise details, declaration dates, and last claim dates before IEPF transfer. Members should verify and claim unclaimed dividends for fiscals 2019, 2022, 2023, and 2024 via KFIN before the deadlines. Reminders were sent in August 2024 and March 2025 with forms to simplify claims.

nodes.title: Transfer of underlying equity shares to the IEPF
nodes.summary: The text covers transfer of unclaimed equity shares to the IEPF under Sections 124 and 125, including reminder letters sent in May 2024 and 14,02,191 shares transferred by 31 March 2025. It provides guidelines for claiming dividends/shares from IEPF via the bank's website. Dematerialisation details include folio and share counts for physical and demat holdings, noting no physical shares were transferred in the last three fiscal years and initiatives in fiscal 2025 to encourage dematerialisation. The Unclaimed Suspense Account section describes transfer of unclaimed sub-divided share certificates, three reminders sent, and a table showing changes in shareholder and share counts during the year, including transfers to IEPF. It notes voting rights on suspense account shares remain frozen until claimed.

nodes.title: Dividend/IEPF Claim Guidelines and Share Dematerialisation Status
key_items: Guidelines to claim dividends / shares transferred to IEPF
nodes.summary: The page covers guidelines for claiming dividends or shares transferred to the IEPF, referencing investor FAQs on the Bank's website. It also addresses dematerialisation of shares, noting that equity shares trade on BSE and NSE. It provides statistics on folios and shares held in physical versus demat form, stating no physical shares were transferred in the last three fiscal years. Finally, it mentions initiatives during fiscal 2025, including letters sent in August 2024 and March 2025, to encourage members to dematerialise their physical holdings.

nodes.title: Unclaimed Suspense Account
nodes.summary: The text covers the Unclaimed Suspense Account, detailing the transfer of unclaimed share certificates from fiscal 2015 sub-division, compliance with SEBI Listing Regulations via reminders to members, and a table showing the movement in the suspense account: beginning balance (174 shareholders, 1,32,005 shares), shareholders who approached (21, 15,000 shares), shares transferred (9, 5,500 shares), ending balance (139, 1,09,005 shares), and a note on 17,500 shares transferred to IEPF for 26 shareholders, with voting rights frozen until claimed. It also includes the Distribution of Shareholding as of 31 March 2025, categorized by electronic and physical forms across shareholding ranges from 1-5000 to 100001 and above, with numbers of holders, shares, and percentages, culminating in totals.

nodes.title: Shareholding Pattern
nodes.summary: The text presents the Bank's shareholding pattern as of 31 March 2025, categorizing holdings into promoters, domestic, and foreign shareholders. It details the number of shares and percentage for each category, including sub-categories like mutual funds, insurance, FPIs, and NRIs. Promoter holding (LIC) is 7.91%. Domestic holding totals 42.48%, and foreign holding totals 46.12%. It then lists shareholders holding over 1% equity, providing names, share counts, and percentages for 16 entities, including LIC, mutual funds, GDRs, and government funds. Notes clarify that shareholding is based on PAN and identify the top 10 public shareholders.

nodes.title: Credit Ratings
nodes.summary: The text lists credit ratings for a bank's outstanding debt instruments as of March 31, 2025, from ICRA, CARE, CRISIL, and India Ratings. It details ratings, outlooks, rating actions, and dates for certificates of deposit, infrastructure bonds, Tier II and Tier I (Basel III) bonds, and fixed deposits. Ratings range from A1+ to AAA and AA+, mostly reaffirmed with stable outlooks. It also notes Fitch, Moody's, and S&P ratings for MTN securities: BB+ stable, Baa3 stable, and BBB- positive, respectively.

nodes.title: Investor Services
nodes.summary:
Investor Services
KFIN has been entrusted with the task of administering all aspects relating to investor services for and on behalf of the Bank. KFIN has appropriate systems to ensure that requisite service is provided to the investors of the Bank in accordance with applicable corporate and securities laws as per the adopted service standards.
Investors are requested to write to the Bank or to KFIN for availing any services or may send their correspondence / complaints to shareholders@axisbank.com or einward.ris@kfintech.com.
317Statutory reports
Members can contact KFIN for redressal of queries by visiting https://kprism.kfintech.com for query registration through free identity registration process. Members can submit their queries on the above website which would generate a registration number. For accessing the status / response to the query submitted, the grievance registration number can be used at the option ‘click here to track your grievance’ after 24 hours.

nodes.title: Investor Correspondence / Complaints
nodes.summary: The text details investor complaints and correspondence for fiscal 2025. It reports 26 complaints received from statutory/regulatory authorities (SEBI SCORES, stock exchanges, NSDL/CDSL, MCA, RBI) and members, all redressed with none pending as of March 31, 2025. It also lists 3,255 investor correspondences on topics like dividend warrants, address changes, ECS, name correction, bank mandate, nominee registration, and others, with 3,247 replied and 8 pending. The status was reviewed by the Stakeholders Relationship Committee and Board.

nodes.title: Process for requests related to physical shares
nodes.summary: The text outlines procedures for physical share requests under SEBI regulations, mandating demat-only processing for transfers, transmissions, and transpositions, and requiring RTAs to issue a 'Letter of Confirmation' valid for 120 days; unclaimed securities go to a Suspense Escrow Demat Account. It details forms ISR-4/ISR-5, investor handbook references, dispute resolution via stock exchange arbitration and online ODR, nomination facility provisions under Section 72, and green initiatives for electronic notices.

nodes.title: Corporate Governance: Shareholder Services, Dispute Resolution, Nomination
nodes.summary: The page covers corporate governance topics for shareholders. It details procedures for claiming securities from the Suspense Escrow Demat Account using forms ISR-4/ISR-5, encourages dematerialization of physical shares, and refers members to the investor handbook for various shareholder services. It outlines the arbitration mechanism for disputes between shareholders and RTAs per SEBI circulars, and the online dispute resolution process via the Smart ODR portal. Additionally, it explains the nomination facility under Section 72 of the Act, encourages members to nominate, provides the nomination form source, and notes that nomination is rescinded upon transfer, transmission, or dematerialization of securities.

nodes.title: Green Initiatives
nodes.summary: The text outlines rules for electronic delivery of company notices and annual reports under Rule 18 of Companies Rules 2014, SEBI Listing Regulations, and MCA/SEBI circulars. It states that documents are sent electronically to members who registered email addresses with DPs or the company/RTA; for unregistered or outdated emails, documents are deemed delivered to available records. Members are urged to update email addresses. The Integrated Annual Report and AGM notice for fiscal 2025 are sent only electronically; no physical copies go to unregistered members, who instead receive a letter with a web link. Members can request free physical copies via email, and documents are also on the Bank's website.

nodes.title: Means of Communication
nodes.summary: The text outlines the Bank's communication channels with shareholders and market participants. It covers the approval and disclosure of quarterly/annual financial results to stock exchanges, the Bank's website, and newspapers. It details investor presentations, post-earnings conference calls with available recordings and transcripts, and regular interactions like group meetings and roadshows, including statistics for fiscal 2025. It also mentions official press releases, compliance reports and corporate announcements, the Integrated Annual Report, investor-centric letters/emails/SMS, a designated investor servicing email address, and a shareholders' feedback survey.

nodes.title: Evaluation of RTA Services
nodes.summary:
Evaluation of RTA Services
With a view to enhance and improve shareholder experience, the Stakeholders Relationship Committee of the Board of the Bank, during the fiscal 2024, formally adopted ‘Guidelines to evaluate the services of Registrar & Transfer Agent of the Bank’. These guidelines lay down parameters for annual performance evaluation of the RTA. During fiscal 2025, evaluation was carried out in accordance with the said guidelines.

nodes.title: General Meetings
nodes.summary: The text details the previous three Annual General Meetings (AGMs) held on 29 July 2022, 28 July 2023, and 26 July 2024, all via video conferencing at 10:00 a.m. It lists special resolutions passed at each AGM, including reappointments and appointments of Independent Directors (Girish Paranjpe, Manoj Kohli, N. S. Vishwanathan, Meena Ganesh, G. Padmanabhan) with their DINs, terms, and effective dates; enhancement of borrowing limit to ₹250,000 crores; borrowing/raising funds via debt securities up to ₹35,000 crores; alteration of Articles of Association for debenture trustee nominee director; and raising funds via equity shares/depository receipts up to ₹20,000 crores. It notes no postal ballot is required for the ensuing AGM and no resolutions were rejected by shareholders in the last three years.

nodes.title: Procedure for Postal Ballot
nodes.summary: The text outlines the postal ballot procedure conducted under Sections 110 and 108 of the Act and Rules 22 and 20 of the Companies (Management and Administration) Rules 2014. It notes MCA circulars allowing electronic notice, so physical copies were not sent; members voted via remote e-voting only. Notices were hosted on the Bank's website, stock exchange websites (BSE and NSE), and NSDL's e-voting site, with a newspaper advertisement about dispatch completion. Voting rights were based on paid-up share value as of the cut-off date. A Scrutinizer ensured fairness, submitted a report to the Chairman, and results were disclosed to stock exchanges, published on websites, and displayed at the registered office.

nodes.title: Details of Special Resolution passed through Postal Ballot during fiscal 2025
nodes.summary: The text provides details of a special resolution passed via postal ballot during fiscal 2025, including the notice date (4 April 2024), scrutinizer (CS KVS Subramanyam), approval date (10 May 2024), and a link to the notice and results. It covers the appointment of Pranam Wahi as an Independent Director for four years from 15 February 2024 to 14 February 2028, with vote counts and percentages in favor and against. A note mentions a board meeting on 17 January 2025 proposing a special resolution for re-appointment of Prof. S. Mahendra Dev for a second term from 14 June 2025. It also references additional information on auditors and directors seeking appointment/re-appointment at the ensuing 31st AGM, as per SEBI Listing Regulations, provided in the AGM notice.

nodes.title: Commodity Price Risk or Foreign Exchange Risk and Hedging Activities
nodes.summary: The text addresses commodity price risk and hedging activities per SEBI circular dated November 15, 2018. It states the Bank lacks a commodity risk management policy because it has no exposure to XAU (Gold) or XAG (Silver). The Bank's total commodity exposure in INR is Nil as of March 31, 2025; exposure to various commodities is not applicable. Commodity risks during the year are not applicable, as the Bank did not run trading positions in gold or silver and has no exposure to any other commodity.

nodes.title: Plant Locations
nodes.summary:
Plant Locations
Being a banking company registered under the Banking Regulation Act, 1949, the provisions relating to disclosure of details relating to plant location are not applicable to the Bank.
The Bank operates through a network of branches spread across the length and breadth of the country. As on 31 March, 2025, the Bank had a network of 5,879 domestic branches and extension counters, 13,941 ATMs and cash recycler machines. The list of branches is available on the website of the Bank at https://branch.axisbank.com.
323Statutory reports

nodes.title: Business Responsibility and Sustainability Report
nodes.summary: The text states that Axis Bank has published its Business Responsibility and Sustainability Report (BRSR) for fiscal 2025 as at 31 March 2025, in accordance with SEBI Circular dated 10 May 2021. It also notes that the BRSR Core has been externally assured by SGS India Private Limited with Reasonable Assurance, per SEBI Circular dated 12 July 2023. The BRSR and Assurance Statement are available on the Bank's website, with a URL provided. The text also references page 324 of the Integrated Annual Report 2024-25 and standalone financial statements.

nodes.title: Independent Auditor’s Report
nodes.summary: The Independent Auditor’s Report for Axis Bank Limited’s Standalone Financial Statements for the year ended 31 March 2025 presents the auditors’ opinion that the financial statements give a true and fair view in accordance with the Banking Regulation Act, 1949, Companies Act, 2013, RBI guidelines, and Accounting Standards. It outlines the basis for opinion, including compliance with Standards on Auditing and ethical requirements. Key Audit Matters cover IT systems and controls over financial reporting, and income recognition, asset classification, and provisioning on advances. The report addresses other information, management and board responsibilities, and auditor responsibilities. Other matters note the predecessor auditors’ unmodified opinion for the prior year. The report on other legal and regulatory requirements affirms compliance with applicable laws, proper books of account, branch audits, internal financial controls, litigation disclosures, provisions for foreseeable losses, IEPF transfers, fund flow representations, dividend compliance, and audit trail operation, and is signed by two Chartered Accountant firms.

nodes.title: Independent Auditor's Report on Axis Bank Standalone Financial Statements
nodes.summary: This page presents the Independent Auditor's Report for Axis Bank Limited's Standalone Financial Statements for the year ended 31 March 2025. It includes the Opinion section, where the auditors state that the financial statements give a true and fair view in accordance with the Banking Regulation Act, 1949, Companies Act, 2013, RBI guidelines, and Accounting Standards. The Basis for Opinion section describes the audit conducted under Standards on Auditing, the auditors' independence per ICAI Code of Ethics, and the sufficiency of audit evidence. It also introduces Key Audit Matters, specifically IT Systems and controls over financial reporting, detailing the importance of IT controls and the audit procedures performed, including involvement of specialists and testing of internal controls.

nodes.title: Key Audit Matters
nodes.summary: This text is an Independent Auditor’s Report on Axis Bank Limited’s Standalone Financial Statements for the year ended 31 March 2025. It covers the auditor’s opinion that the statements give a true and fair view in accordance with the Banking Regulation Act, Companies Act, RBI guidelines, and Accounting Standards. It outlines the basis for opinion, including compliance with Standards on Auditing and ethical requirements. The report identifies two Key Audit Matters: (1) Information Technology systems and controls over financial reporting, detailing the audit approach to assess IT control environment, general IT controls, and automated/manual business cycle controls; and (2) Income Recognition, Asset Classification, and Provisioning on Advances (IRAC) per RBI norms, including testing of internal controls, IT systems, and substantive procedures for NPA identification and provisioning. It includes specific figures for total loans and advances and provisions for NPAs.

nodes.title: Other Information
nodes.summary: The text outlines auditor responsibilities regarding 'other information' in the Bank's Annual Report. It states the Board is responsible for this information, which excludes the standalone financial statements and auditor's report, and may be available after the audit report date. The auditor's opinion does not cover it, and no assurance is provided. The auditor must read it when available to check for material inconsistencies with the financial statements or audit knowledge, and if a material misstatement is found, communicate to those charged with governance and take appropriate legal action.

nodes.title: Responsibilities of Management and Those Charged with Governance for the Standalone Financial Statements
nodes.summary: The text outlines management and board responsibilities for standalone financial statements under section 134(5) of the Act, including preparation that gives a true and fair view of state of affairs, profit, and cash flows per Accounting Standards, Companies Rules 2021, Banking Regulation Act section 29, and RBI guidelines. Responsibilities include maintaining adequate accounting records, safeguarding assets, preventing fraud, selecting compliant accounting software with audit logs, applying appropriate accounting policies, making reasonable judgments and estimates, and designing effective internal financial controls. It also covers assessing going concern ability, disclosing related matters, and using going concern basis unless liquidation or cessation is intended. The board oversees financial reporting.

nodes.title: Auditor’s Responsibilities for the Audit of the Standalone Financial Statements
nodes.summary: The text outlines the auditor's responsibilities for auditing standalone financial statements. It covers objectives: obtaining reasonable assurance against material misstatement from fraud or error and issuing an opinion. It details professional judgment and skepticism, risk identification and assessment (noting higher fraud risk), understanding internal controls and opining on their adequacy and effectiveness, evaluating accounting policies and estimates, assessing going concern appropriateness and related disclosures, and evaluating overall presentation and fair presentation. It also covers communication with those charged with governance regarding audit scope, timing, findings, internal control deficiencies, independence compliance, and determination of key audit matters for the auditor's report, subject to disclosure exceptions.

nodes.title: Other Matters
nodes.summary:
Other Matters
16. Attention is drawn to the fact that the Standalone Financial Statements of the Bank for the year ended 31 March 2024 were audited by predecessor auditors whose report dated 24 April 2024 expressed an unmodified opinion on those Standalone Financial Statements.

nodes.title: Report on Other Legal and Regulatory Requirements
nodes.summary: This auditor's report on a bank's standalone financial statements covers compliance with the Banking Regulation Act and Companies Act. It affirms receipt of necessary information, confirms transactions are within the bank's powers, and details a centralized audit with visits to 92 branches. It states proper books were kept, financial statements agree with books, and comply with accounting standards. It confirms no director disqualifications, refers to a separate annexure on internal financial controls, notes Section 197 doesn't apply, discloses pending litigation, provisions for foreseeable losses, timely transfer to the Investor Education and Protection Fund, management representations on no undisclosed fund flows, dividend compliance, and proper audit trail operation. Signed by two Chartered Accountant firms.

nodes.title: Annexure ‘A’ to the Independent Auditors’ report on the Standalone Financial Statements of Axis Bank Limited for the year ended 31 March 2025
key_items: Opinion; Management’s responsibility for Internal Financial Controls; Auditor’s responsibility
Management’s responsibility for Internal Financial Controls
Meaning of Internal Financial Controls with reference to the Standalone Financial Statements
Inherent Limitations of Internal Financial Controls with reference to the Standalone Financial Statements
nodes.summary: This annexure to the Independent Auditors' report covers the audit of Axis Bank's internal financial controls over financial reporting for the year ended 31 March 2025. It includes the auditors' opinion that the controls were adequate and operating effectively, management's responsibility for establishing and maintaining such controls, and the auditors' responsibility and procedures. It also explains the meaning and inherent limitations of internal financial controls. The document concludes with auditor signatures and the standalone balance sheet as at 31 March 2025, showing capital and liabilities, assets, contingent liabilities, and bills for collection, with comparative figures for 2024.

nodes.title: Standalone Profit and Loss Account
nodes.summary: The text presents a standalone profit and loss account for the year ended 31 March 2025, with comparative figures for 2024. It details income (interest earned, other income), expenditure (interest expended, operating expenses, provisions and contingencies), net profit, balance brought forward, and amounts available for appropriation. Appropriations include transfers to various reserves (statutory, capital, special, investment, investment fluctuation), dividend paid, and balance carried to the balance sheet. Earnings per equity share (basic and diluted) are provided. Referenced schedules and significant accounting policies are noted. Auditor and director signatures are included, along with company details and financial statement page number.

nodes.summary: This standalone cash flow statement for the year ended 31 March 2025, with comparatives for 2024, presents cash flows from operating, investing, and financing activities. Operating activities include adjustments for depreciation, mark-to-market losses, provisions, and changes in working capital, plus direct taxes paid. Investing activities cover purchase of fixed assets, acquisition of Citibank India consumer business, held-to-maturity investments, subsidiary investments, and proceeds from asset sales. Financing activities include subordinated debt and AT1 issuances/repayments, borrowings changes, share capital proceeds, and dividend payments. It also shows exchange fluctuation effects, net increase in cash, opening and closing cash balances, and notes on cash components and CSR spending. Auditor signatures and board approvals are included.

nodes.title: Schedules forming part of the Balance Sheet
nodes.summary: The section includes schedules forming part of the Balance Sheet as of 31 March 2025 and 31 March 2024, in thousands of rupees. It covers Schedule 1 (Capital), Schedule 1A (Employee Stock Options Outstanding), Schedule 2 (Reserves and Surplus), Schedule 3 (Deposits), Schedule 4 (Borrowings), Schedule 5 (Other Liabilities and Provisions), Schedule 6 (Cash and Balances with RBI), Schedule 7 (Balances with Banks and Money at Call and Short Notice), Schedule 8 (Investments), Schedule 9 (Advances), Schedule 10 (Fixed Assets), Schedule 11 (Other Assets), and Schedule 12 (Contingent Liabilities). Each schedule provides detailed breakdowns, comparative figures for both years, and explanatory notes on items such as secured borrowings, subordinated debt, additional tier I bonds, pledged securities, priority sector shortfall deposits, and contingent liabilities.

nodes.title: Schedule 1A - Employees’ Stock Options Outstanding
nodes.summary: The text presents balance sheet schedules as of 31 March 2025, covering Schedule 1 - Capital, which details authorised capital of 4,250,000,000 equity shares of ₹2 each (₹8,500,000 thousand) for both years, and issued, subscribed and paid-up capital of 3,097,369,066 shares (₹6,194,738 thousand) versus prior year's 3,086,570,375 shares (₹6,173,141 thousand). Schedule 1A - Employees’ Stock Options Outstanding shows opening balance, additions, deductions, and closing balance in thousands for both years, with footnotes explaining additions as cost recognized in P&L and recovered from group entities, and deductions as amounts transferred to Share Premium on exercise and General Reserve on lapses.
